content: Does anyone have in mind any good candidates for things we could try and a to formalise in PhyslibAlpha? Maybe these are things in physics that people have wanted to see been formalised in physics but haven’t had the time to or more generally cool results from physics which would be good to have part of the PhysLib echo system?
In particular it would be nice to see some API-maps developed for these areas, and then we could perhaps make a tool like Tau Ceti’s command-line tool that fills these in as part of PhyslibAlpha.
As an experiment for tau ceti style development we could maybe start with the classical mechanics and geometric mechanics and try methods like tau ceti has to fill this in.

A bit of an aside, but I have had a few thoughts about this while working on the QM side of Physlib.

First, I think it would be useful to work out a broader roadmap/API with some concrete goals, and ideally discuss this among everyone interested in contributing to an area. At least in quantum mechanics, my impression is that people currently have quite different ideas of what the development should look like. For example, Alex Meiburg, Gregory Loges and I seem to be working in rather different directions. There is nothing wrong with someone focusing only on finite-dimensional QM, for example, but I think it would still be valuable to agree on a general framework into which these different developments are supposed to fit.

Related to this is the question of how general we want results in Physlib to be. For hydrogen, one could write down the eigenfunctions and prove directly that they solve the Schrödinger equation, or one could develop the underlying SO(4) symmetry and understand the eigenspaces through irreducible representations. Similarly, one could formalise the classical 1D harmonic oscillator on ℝ directly, or aim for results in classical mechanics that are formulated intrinsically on symplectic manifolds. Maybe the answer is simply that all of these approaches are welcome, but from a theoretical-physics perspective I personally find the more structural/abstract results much more interesting, especially when concrete examples can then be recovered as applications.

A second, somewhat separate issue is AI-assisted development. Out of curiosity, and also to get a feeling for how far one can push towards a reasonably complete treatment of infinite-dimensional QM, I let an agent work on this for about 48 hours. It produced roughly 80 files and 30k+ lines of Lean. The results include the unbounded spectral theorem, Stone’s theorem, Lindblad generators and quantum semigroups, and essentially solving the hydrogen atom and harmonic oscillator at a fairly general level.

I am actually not quite sure what to do with this now. I could clean it up to some extent and put the whole development into PhyslibAlpha.

For my normal, much smaller agent runs, I have instead been extracting small PRs, usually at most ~300 lines, checking them myself and trying to make sure the code is reasonably up to standard. That works, but it is painstakingly slow, and I locally have many results that at this speed will take weeks to push.

One problem I keep running into is that agents tend to produce proofs that are much longer and more complicated than necessary. If anyone has experimented with an agent-based workflow specifically for cleaning up, shortening and refactoring generated Lean after the fact, I would be very interested in trying that.

So those are some of the things I have been wondering about: what common roadmap/API we want developments to converge towards, how general we want the results to be and whether PhyslibAlpha could also be useful as a place for these much larger experimental agent-generated developments.

Many different seperate points in your message, will try to respond to each one.

  1. It would be great if people organized around projects around different sub fields of physics and work on API maps/road maps as you have said. However, projects like physlib are very volunteer driven so schedules are difficult to align; therefore it usually ends up with people working on different paths with the hope that we each grapple with how to make this connect and the reviewing part also aims to make this connection happen. The API maps also can help with this as each contributor can figure out how the parts they are interested in can fit in.

  2. I would presume we want all levels of generality as long as its mainstream, for example in some areas of classical mechanics, there is 1D work and also geometric mechanics being developed (albeit the latter at a slow rate), the goal would be to at each step, 'prove' that the following abstractions are equivalent.

  3. This is also one of the issues that I face with AI myself but I believe it is important to keep in mind that the pushing PR's to physlib is only part of contributing, the other equally important parts being reviewing and maintaining the code. As you have experienced AI is not able to produce code on the level that physlib requires and again I also have to spend much longer understanding the proofs and arguments and refactoring everything. But I have come to accept that this is just the process that it takes, AI can show you that what you want might be true, but polishing this code is in fact the harder and more useful part and it takes as long as it takes :(. But now I also find it satisfying to polish code as it really helps me understand the physics (and sometimes the math) being formalized, but I wonder if physlibalpha would be the place for the large, extremely slow AI code, as it would just grow uncontrollably if that is the standard we set.

I let an agent work on this for about 48 hours. It produced roughly 80 files and 30k+ lines of Lean. The results include the unbounded spectral theorem, Stone’s theorem, Lindblad generators and quantum semigroups, and essentially solving the hydrogen atom and harmonic oscillator at a fairly general level.

I think the important question here is: Would having those 30k+ lines in PhyslibAlpha be helpful to someone else. E.g. Is it something others can understand, navigate around, and develop further. Or is the vast majority of it just unreadable code aimed at hitting certain goals. I suspect it is that latter in this case (but please correct me if I'm wrong), but if it happened to be the former, then I think there is some worth having it - with the understanding that it would be developed further, etc.

Here is an example of something I put into PhyslibAlpha, Physlib#1357. It's about 2000 lines of human-guided AI generated code. I think part of the unwritten goal with PhyslibAlpha is to come up with enough linters and controls so that, beyond the physics, the code going into it is somewhat of a good quality.

Would be very open to peoples opinions on this though.

I actually think this would be an ok contribution to PhyslibAlpha. Though would swap the directory structure around and integrate the Harmonic oscillator stuff with things already in PhyslibAlpha. I think a good catchphrase might be:

PhyslibAlpha exists for the rapid development of physics formalizations, enabled by a lighter review process built to handle large-scale, human- or AI-generated contributions
Related Physlib#1596

Another candidate area for PhyslibAlpha could be fluid dynamics and PDE analysis, building on the basic Navier–Stokes and Euler definitions already in Physlib. An agent-based workflow could start with an API-map focused on concrete stepping stones: verifying exact solutions and energy dissipation like Poiseuille flow, Taylor–Green vortices, and 2D enstrophy conservation, followed by the 1D Burgers' equation via Cole–Hopf, stationary Stokes via Lax–Milgram, and Kato-style mild L³ solutions. It would be interesting to see how much of that progression an automated pipeline could scaffold and fill in.
@Dan You think it would be easy to fill out an API-map with some of these?

In addition to the above suggestions: Here there was some discussion on lattice QFT, #Natural sciences > Finite-volume lattice-gauge cluster expansion in Lean 4. I think this would also be nice to include. I have some hand-written code on lattice QFT I did a while back, in a different direction to these projects. Though collectively these superseded what I did.
